# Response and Resistance to RAS inhibition in Cancer

**Authors:** Richard Y. Ebright; Julien Dilly; Alice T. Shaw; Andrew J. Aguirre

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Medical Oncology, Dana Farber Cancer Institute, Boston, MA, 02115, USA | 2Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, 02115, USA | 3Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, Cambridge, MA, 02142, USA

## Abstract

RAS inhibition has the potential to transform cancer treatment for many patients. The landscape of RAS inhibitor therapies is rapidly evolving, with two mutant-selective KRAS inhibitors now approved and multiple other mutant-selective, pan-KRAS, and pan-RAS inhibitors in development. However, monotherapy efficacy has been limited by primary and acquired resistance. Here, we review preclinical and clinical data on RAS inhibition in cancer and describe multiple genetic and non-genetic mechanisms of resistance. Moreover, we highlight future opportunities for the design of rational combination therapy strategies, which will ultimately be needed to overcome resistance and enhance the efficacy of these promising treatments.

## Introduction

RAS oncoproteins have long been known to be key drivers of cancer initiation and progression. RAS proteins are small GTPases that regulate cell growth and proliferation, acting as molecular switches and cycling between GTP-bound “ON” and GDP-bound “OFF” states. Once in the GTP-bound ON state, the RAS proteins mediate signaling from upstream receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) to downstream effector signaling molecules, most notably triggering activation of the MAPK and PI3K pathways (Figure 1A). Besides their key involvement in MAPK and PI3K signaling, the RAS proteins activate a host of other effector signaling molecules to regulate a variety of cellular processes (1).

Given their central role in cell proliferation and survival, it is no surprise that RAS genes are among the most commonly mutated genes in cancer. Nearly 20% of cancer cases have activating mutations in one of three main RAS proteins, including KRAS, NRAS, and HRAS (2). These mutations cause RAS proteins to preferentially be in the ON state, resulting in increased signaling that promotes growth and proliferation, even in the absence of upstream RTK signals. KRAS is the most commonly altered RAS gene, with recurrent oncogenic mutations occurring at several positions, including codons 12, 13 and 61, as well as genetic amplification of either mutant or wild type (WT) alleles (3). For decades, scientists sought to develop small molecule inhibitors of oncogenic KRAS; however, KRAS lacks deep binding pockets, limiting small molecule binding, and KRAS has a high affinity for GTP and GDP, making it difficult to develop drugs that could displace these molecules. In 2013, however, Shokat and colleagues reported the identification of a novel allosteric pocket, termed the “switch II” pocket, located between the switch II domain, the α3-helix, and the central β-sheet of RAS (4). Moreover, they were able to identify small molecules that occupied this pocket and covalently bound to the mutant cysteine at position 12 in the GDP-bound OFF form of the KRASG12C oncoprotein. By covalently binding to the KRASG12C protein and locking it in the OFF state, these small molecules were able to selectively inhibit oncogenic signaling from mutant KRAS while sparing WT KRAS (5,6). These initial reports ultimately led to the development of multiple inhibitors of the KRASG12C OFF state (7–9). Two of these early KRASG12C (OFF) inhibitors, sotorasib and adagrasib, are now approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for use in advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and colorectal cancer (CRC). Moreover, many additional small molecule inhibitors of RAS proteins are now in preclinical and clinical development, including agents specific to other mutant KRAS alleles, pan-KRAS, and pan-RAS inhibitors (Table 1).

Unfortunately, clinical efficacy of KRAS inhibitors has been limited by both primary and acquired resistance to monotherapy. While most patients have clinical benefit in the form of stable disease (SD) or partial responses (PR) from KRAS inhibitors, complete responses (CRs) are rare. Moreover, most responses are short-lived, and acquired resistance inevitably develops, leading to resumption of tumor growth despite treatment. Additionally, a significant number of patients demonstrate primary resistance to monotherapy and have progressive disease (PD) on treatment. Both clinical and preclinical studies have suggested a variety of mechanisms by which cancer cells become resistant to KRAS inhibitors (10–16). These putative resistance mechanisms include, among others, mutations in KRAS preventing drug binding, alterations within the RAS-MAPK or PI3K signaling pathways, malignant cell state changes, and metabolic changes (Figure 1B). While additional studies are necessary to quantify the effect of each of these mechanisms on drug resistance, the recurrent nature across multiple different patients or model systems and the known role of many altered genes in the RAS signaling pathway suggest important contributions for these events in driving drug resistance.

Given the inevitable development of resistance to KRAS inhibitors, combination regimens will be needed to improve the depth and durability of clinical responses. Here, we will describe the efficacy of RAS inhibition in the clinic, current knowledge of mechanisms of resistance to RAS inhibition, and a framework for thinking about the rational development of combination therapies for RAS inhibitors. It took roughly 3 decades from the discovery of KRAS to the development of the first small molecule inhibitor of KRAS. Eight years later, the first clinical approval of a KRAS inhibitor occurred. Development of next-generation RAS inhibitors with improved potency, selectivity, and pharmacokinetic properties, as well as design of effective combination therapy with RAS inhibitors will need to proceed even more quickly to unleash the full potential of these powerful drugs to benefit patients.

### Targeting RAS in the clinic

#### KRASG12C inhibitors

#### NSCLC

The first successes of targeting KRAS in the clinic were with the KRASG12C inhibitors sotorasib and adagrasib. Both molecules take advantage of the mutated cysteine at position 12 to selectively and covalently bind to mutant KRAS, and both molecules are KRASG12C (OFF) inhibitors, binding to GDP-bound, inactive KRAS and preventing displacement of GDP and subsequent KRAS activation. Both sotorasib and adagrasib were initially tested in patients with NSCLC, the disease with the highest rate of KRASG12C mutations (10–13% of all cases). Initial clinical proof-of-concept was demonstrated in the Phase 1/2 CodeBreaK 100 trial, in which sotorasib demonstrated an objective response rate (ORR) of 41.0% and median progression-free survival (mPFS) of 6.3 months in advanced KRASG12C mutated NSCLC patients who had received prior chemotherapy (17). Soon after, adagrasib similarly demonstrated an ORR of 42.9% and mPFS of 6.5 months in advanced NSCLC in the Phase 1/2 KRYSTAL-1 trial (18). These data led the FDA to grant accelerated approval for sotorasib in May 2021 and for adagrasib in December 2022 for the treatment of advanced, previously treated KRASG12C NSCLC, marking the first ever approvals of KRAS inhibitors. Importantly, confirmatory Phase 3 trials are required for the FDA to grant full approval for both agents. In the randomized Phase 3 CodeBreaK 200 trial comparing sotorasib to docetaxel, sotorasib demonstrated a statistically significant increase in mPFS (5.6 months vs 4.5 months), but failed to demonstrate an increase in overall survival (OS) (10.6 months vs 11.3 months) (19). This was partially attributed to a high rate of patient dropout on the docetaxel arm of the trial (20), and the FDA has required an additional confirmatory Phase 3 trial for full approval of sotorasib. In the randomized Phase 3 KRYSTAL-12 trial comparing adagrasib to docetaxel, adagrasib demonstrated a statistically significant increase in mPFS (5.5 months vs 3.8 months); OS has not yet been reported. The full development of KRASG12C inhibitors has been recently covered in more detail elsewhere (21).

#### CRC

Given the frequency of KRASG12C mutations in CRC (3–4% of all cases), both sotorasib and adagrasib were also evaluated in this disease. In the CRC arm of the CodeBreaK 100 trial, sotorasib demonstrated a modest ORR of 9.7% and mPFS of 4.0 months (22); similar results were seen in the CRC arm of the KRYSTAL-1 trial, with adagrasib demonstrating an ORR of 18.6% and mPFS of 5.6 months (23). Given the lack of effective treatment options for advanced chemotherapy-resistant CRC, these monotherapy results were still promising, although less impressive than those responses seen in NSCLC.

CRC is known to have significant EGFR expression and pathway activation, and anti-EGFR antibodies (cetuximab, panitumumab) are approved for use in RAS/RAFWT CRC. In BRAF-mutant CRC, preclinical studies suggested that adaptive reactivation of EGFR can limit the efficacy of MAPK pathway inhibition (24,25). Combined BRAF and EGFR blockade with anti-EGFR monoclonal antibodies in clinical trials demonstrated significantly greater clinical benefit than BRAF inhibition alone, leading to establishment of combined BRAF inhibition and anti-EGFR therapy as a standard-of-care (26–28). Similarly, preclinical studies demonstrated that EGFR signaling also serves as an adaptive response to KRAS inhibition in CRC, suggesting that combined KRAS and EGFR inhibition could have increased efficacy (29,30). Adding EGFR inhibition to KRAS therapy indeed proved efficacious, and the combination of adagrasib and cetuximab in the CRC arm of the KRYSTAL-1 trial demonstrated an ORR of 34.0% and mPFS of 6.9 months, leading to accelerated approval of the combination in June 2024 for the treatment of KRASG12C CRC (15). In the Phase 3 CodeBreaK 300 trial, the combination of sotorasib and panitumumab demonstrated an ORR of 26.4% and mPFS 5.6 months, representing significant increases over the standard-of-care comparator arm of trifluridine-tipiracil or regorafenib (ORR 0%, mPFS 2.2 months) (31); this combination was approved in January 2025. Recent data with divarasib and cetuximab in KRASG12C CRC suggest even greater efficacy, with a reported ORR of 62.5% and mPFS of 8.1 months (32). Targeting this adaptive feedback signaling through EGFR and other RTKs remains an active area of clinical investigation, with trials ongoing utilizing RTK blockade or inhibition of downstream signaling nodes such as other WT RAS isoforms.

#### PDAC

Multiple KRASG12C inhibitors have also demonstrated promising results in other KRASG12C tumors across different cancer lineages. Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is one of the most treatment-refractory cancer types, and over 90% of tumors have KRAS mutations; however, only a small percentage (1–2%) harbor KRASG12C mutations. Recent clinical trials of KRASG12C inhibitors have shown promising results in PDAC patients who had progressed on prior chemotherapy. In a Phase 1/2 trial, sotorasib demonstrated an ORR of 21.1% and mPFS of 4.0 months (33), and in a Phase 2 trial, adagrasib demonstrated an ORR of 33.3% and mPFS of 5.4 months (34). Early data from Phase 1 studies of multiple other KRASG12C inhibitors have included small numbers of patients with PDAC with an ORR of approximately 40%. These results with KRASG12C inhibitors in PDAC have provided valuable proof-of-concept for KRAS inhibition in PDAC and compare favorably to standard-of-care chemotherapies in the second-line setting, which have consistently shown ORRs of less than 10% and mPFS of only a few months (35,36). These results have led to both sotorasib and adagrasib being included in National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines for consideration of use in patients with KRASG12C PDAC.

#### Other cancer types

In addition to NSCLC, CRC, and PDAC, low rates of KRASG12C mutations are observed in other tumor types, including appendiceal, anal, cholangiocarcinoma, gastric, large cell neuroendocrine, and melanoma. For example, in a Phase 2 cohort of the KRYSTAL-1 study, adagrasib monotherapy was evaluated in patients with advanced KRASG12C cancer types, excluding NSCLC and CRC (34). Responses were observed in 5/12 (41.7%) cholangiocarcinoma, 1/3 (33%) gastroesophageal, 2/4 (50%) ovarian, and 2/3 (66.7%) endometrial cancers.

#### KRASG12C inhibitors in development

Beyond the approved KRASG12C inhibitors, multiple next-generation KRASG12C inhibitors comprising a variety of mechanisms-of-action (MOAs) are also in development with a goal to improve potency, target coverage, clinical efficacy, and tolerability (Table 1). Divarasib is a KRASG12C (OFF) inhibitor with increased potency and selectivity for KRASG12C (37) which has demonstrated greater monotherapy response rates than sotorasib and adagrasib in a Phase 1 study treating patients with NSCLC (ORR 53%) and CRC (ORR 29%) (12). Moreover, the combination of divarasib plus cetuximab resulted in an ORR of 62.5% in KRASG12C inhibitor-naive patients with advanced CRC (32). Divarasib is presently being evaluated in multiple ongoing studies, including a Phase 3 study in NSCLC. Similarly, D3S-001 is a KRASG12C (OFF) inhibitor with more potent and rapid target engagement, with encouraging early clinical data, including an ORR of 73.5% in a relatively small cohort of 34 KRASG12C inhibitor-naïve NSCLC, CRC, and PDAC patients (38,39). Importantly, responses were observed in 8/9 (89%) CRC and 3/4 (75%) PDAC patients (39). At least 10 other KRASG12C (OFF) inhibitors are also in early clinical trials (Table 1).

Elironrasib (previously RMC-6291) works by a distinct MOA and is a KRASG12C (ON) inhibitor, which blocks the GTP-bound “ON” form of the protein. Elironrasib binds to KRASG12C (ON) through a molecular glue mechanism, forming a “tri-complex” with cyclophilin A (CYPA) and covalently binding to the mutant cysteine at position 12, resulting in steric inhibition of KRAS from interacting with effector proteins (40). Elironrasib has demonstrated preliminary efficacy in Phase 1 studies, including ORRs of 43% and 40% in KRASG12C inhibitor-naïve NSCLC and CRC, respectively; notably, elironrasib has also shown efficacy (ORR 50%) in NSCLC patients previously treated with KRASG12C (OFF) inhibitors (41).

Finally, BBO-8520 is a recently-described dual KRASG12C (ON/OFF) inhibitor which binds in the switch II pocket regardless of whether KRAS is bound to GTP or GDP; preclinical studies demonstrated this dual ON/OFF inhibition leads to greater target engagement and KRAS inhibition than that of sotorasib or adagrasib, as well as efficacy in sotorasib-resistant tumor models (42). BBO-8520 is being evaluated in a Phase 1 clinical trial.

#### KRASG12D inhibitors

In addition to KRASG12C inhibitors, there are now multiple inhibitors of other mutant KRAS alleles in clinical development, primarily focused on KRASG12D, which is found in approximately 4% of NSCLC, 10% of CRC, and 40% of PDAC patients, and for which the mutant aspartate in the KRASG12D protein provides key interactions to enhance binding potency (43,44). These clinical agents represent multiple distinct MOAs (Table 1). MRTX1133 is a KRASG12D (OFF) inhibitor that is structurally similar to adagrasib and gains mutant selectivity via noncovalent binding to the mutant aspartic acid (45). While this molecule has been instrumental to many important studies of KRAS inhibition in preclinical models, suboptimal pharmacokinetic properties have led to halted clinical development of this compound (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05737706; RRID:SCR_002309). Zoldonrasib (previously RMC-9805) is a KRASG12D (ON) inhibitor that is structurally similar to elironrasib, forming an inhibitory tri-complex with GTP-bound KRASG12D and gaining mutant selectivity via covalent binding to the mutant aspartic acid (46). Early clinical data from the Phase 1 study of zoldonrasib have demonstrated objective responses in approximately 30% of PDAC patients, with evidence of excellent safety (47). Given the high frequency of KRASG12D mutations across many human cancer types, KRASG12D-selective inhibitors hold great potential to benefit patients.

#### Pan-(K)RAS inhibitors

The above inhibitors demonstrate mutant selectivity, which should increase the therapeutic window by inhibiting mutant KRAS while sparing WT KRAS. However, pan-KRAS inhibitors targeting all KRAS isoforms (both mutant and WT) and pan-RAS inhibitors targeting all RAS isoforms (K-/H-/NRAS, both mutant and WT) may have several advantages, including broader clinical applicability across a spectrum of patients with different mechanisms of RAS pathway activation, such as RAS mutations, amplifications, and upstream RTK alterations. Moreover, pan-(K)RAS inhibitors hold the potential to prevent some drug resistance mechanisms caused by on-target RAS mutations or reactivation of WT RAS activity. These advantages will need to be balanced against the projected risk of greater systemic toxicity compared with mutant-selective agents.

#### pan-KRAS inhibitors

Many pan-KRAS inhibitors that target mutant and WT KRAS with selectivity over HRAS and NRAS are currently in development (Table 1). BI-3706674 is a noncovalent pan-KRAS (OFF) inhibitor, with activity against multiple KRAS-mutant alleles, but which spares NRAS and HRAS. BI-3706674 (and tool compound BI-2865) has activity against a range of mutants, including G12C, G12D, G12V, G13D, and Q61H, among others, as well as WT KRAS. Selectivity for KRAS is derived from binding to the H95 residue in the α3 helix of KRAS, which is not shared with NRAS or HRAS (48). This pan-KRAS approach could have broad applicability across multiple KRAS-mutant alleles, while avoiding toxicity from WT NRAS or HRAS inhibition by pan-RAS inhibitors. Additionally, preclinical studies have suggested that these pan-KRAS (OFF) inhibitors may also be more effective than pan-RAS (ON) inhibitors in KRAS WT amplified tumors, perhaps due in part to the propensity of WT KRAS to cycle into the OFF state (49). BI-3706674 is now being studied in a Phase 1 clinical trial. Moreover, multiple other pan-KRAS inhibitors targeting the GTP- and/or GDP-bound forms of the protein are in late preclinical or early clinical development.

#### pan-RAS inhibitors

Daraxonrasib (previously RMC-6236) is a noncovalent tri-complex RAS (ON) multi-selective inhibitor, with activity against mutant and WT KRAS, NRAS, and HRAS proteins (50,51). Daraxonrasib, as well as the related preclinical compound RMC-7977, works by reversibly recruiting CYPA to the GTP-bound, active state of RAS, thus serving as a molecular glue to form a tri-complex that prevents RAS (ON) from binding to its effectors. Additionally, these inhibitors have also been shown to work through a second MOA by induction of alterations in switch II residues in RAS to stimulate GTP hydrolysis, thereby promoting the transition to inactive RAS (52). Extensive preclinical studies have demonstrated the efficacy of daraxonrasib and RMC-7977 across a spectrum of RAS-mutant tumor models (50,51,53). Despite potent activity on WT RAS proteins, RMC-7977 and daraxonrasib have shown acceptable tolerability in these preclinical models, suggesting that these pan-RAS (ON) inhibitors may leverage a therapeutic window created by oncogene addiction to active GTP-bound RAS in tumor cells compared to WT cells. Early clinical data for daraxonrasib have been promising in NSCLC and PDAC. For example, in early Phase 1 data in second-line PDAC patients with KRASG12X mutations, daraxonrasib achieved an ORR of 29% and mPFS of 8.5 months (54). Similarly, in early Phase 1 data in NSCLC patients with KRASG12X mutations who had received 1–2 lines of prior therapy, daraxonrasib achieved an ORR of 38% and mPFS of 9.8 months (55). On the other hand, daraxonrasib monotherapy has shown relatively limited efficacy in a small cohort of patients with RAS-mutant CRC treated with a 300 mg daily dose, with an ORR of only 9% (2/22) recently reported (55). While daraxonrasib binds potently to both mutant and WT RAS, this monotherapy efficacy in KRAS-mutant CRC is considerably less than the combination efficacy observed with mutant-selective KRASG12C inhibitors plus anti-EGFR antibodies, thus suggesting that, in CRC patients, daraxonrasib alone may not sufficiently block adaptive signaling through WT RAS at achievable exposures with the 300 mg dose and/or that addition of anti-EGFR antibodies may have added benefit beyond blockade of EGFR-mediated activation of WT RAS. Perhaps surprisingly, despite inhibiting WT K/H/NRAS, toxicity from daraxonrasib monotherapy has typically been manageable in patients, with generally low-grade rash, GI distress, and mucositis as the primary adverse events. Based on these data, daraxonrasib has advanced to multiple Phase 3 trials comparing daraxonrasib to standard-of-care chemotherapy in 2L PDAC and NSCLC, as well as Phase 1/2 combination therapy studies. Beyond daraxonrasib, there are now several other pan-RAS inhibitors in clinical development, as well, including LUNA18 and YL-17231 (Table 1), and additional pan-RAS inhibitors in preclinical development, such as ERAS-0015.

#### KRAS degraders

Targeted protein degradation is an alternative strategy for KRAS therapeutics. Degraders coopt cellular proteolysis machinery by bringing an E3 ligase to a target protein of interest, leading to ubiquitination of the target protein and subsequent proteosome-mediated degradation. If the degrader binds to the target protein noncovalently, the molecule is generally not broken down in this process and is instead recycled (56). Importantly, unlike small molecule inhibitors, degraders act catalytically, suggesting that small quantities of intracellular drug could have significant effects on total target protein levels.

Preclinical data support a role for elimination of KRAS protein through KRAS degradation as an effective modality of targeted therapy. Studies in genetically engineered mouse models (GEMM) models of oncogenic Kras-driven lung cancer compared the efficacy and emergence of resistance between genetic ablation of KrasG12V expression in a KrasG12V;Trp53-mutant GEMM and pharmacologic inhibition in the KrasG12C;Trp53-mutant GEMM using sotorasib (57). Genetic ablation using Cre-recombinase technology of KrasG12V led to robust antiproliferative activity and induction of apoptosis, with complete regression of tumors and no recurrence observed in most mice. Pharmacologic inhibition of KrasG12C resulted in more modest response rates, and acquired resistance occurred in all mice. Furthermore, recent work using the degradation tag (dTAG) system in KrasG12V transgenic mouse models demonstrated that acute degradation of KrasG12V led to regression of lung and pancreatic cancers in mice, with disruption of RAS-MAPK signaling and increased T cell infiltration within the TME (58). A second report evaluating KrasG12V degradation with the dTAG system in a mouse model of lung cancer also demonstrated rapid tumor regressions and immune remodeling upon degradation (https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.12.13.627539v1; RRID:SCR_003933).

Both mutant-selective and pan-KRAS degraders have been described in the literature. One of the first reported KRAS degraders was LC-2, a proteolysis-targeting chimera (PROTAC) molecule, with a VHL E3 ligase-binding domain connected via a linker to a KRASG12C-binding domain based on adagrasib; notably, because adagrasib covalently binds to KRASG12C, this molecule gets degraded with its target, preventing catalytic activity (59). Additionally, the pan-KRAS PROTAC degrader ACBI3 was designed based on recently described pan-KRAS inhibitors and was reported to potently degrade WT and many (but not all) different mutant KRAS proteins (48,60,61). The only KRAS degrader with clinical data to date is ASP3082, which is an intravenously administered KRASG12D degrader (62). Preliminary data with ASP3082 included responses in PDAC and NSCLC, but an ORR of only 8% across all doses and cancer types tested, suggesting that KRAS degradation can lead to tumor shrinkage but will likely need additional molecule and/or dose optimization to be clinically viable (63). The same company also has a second KRASG12D degrader in Phase 1 clinical trials, ASP4396, which reportedly links KRASG12D to a different, undisclosed E3 ligase (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06364696; RRID:SCR_002309).

Targeted protein degradation remains an active area of preclinical and clinical investigation, yet important questions remain, including whether degrader molecules can be sufficiently optimized to potently and completely degrade RAS proteins while having good oral bioavailability and drug exposure and whether degradation of KRAS has meaningful advantages over complete inhibition in patients. In theory, pan-KRAS degradation could prevent emergence of other oncogenic KRAS alleles that have been seen at acquired resistance with mutant-selective KRASG12C inhibitors (e.g., G12V, G12D); however, drug-specific binding site mutations would still be anticipated to arise with KRAS degraders, and novel mechanisms of resistance may also emerge, such as dysregulation of proteolysis machinery, as has been recently described (https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.12.13.627539v1; RRID:SCR_003933). Moreover, a large array of genetic and non-genetic resistance mechanisms to KRAS inhibition have been described that would cause resistance irrespective of the modality of RAS targeting (inhibition or degradation), such as mutations downstream of RAS in the MAPK pathway (e.g., BRAF mutation) and cell state alterations leading to drug resistance (e.g., epithelial-mesenchymal transition). Given these considerations, development of next-generation, potent, and orally bioavailable small molecule RAS inhibitors and rationally designed combination therapy strategies may currently be the more rapid and impactful strategy for RAS-targeted therapeutics.

#### Advancing RAS inhibition to earlier lines of therapy

Most clinical trials for RAS inhibitors have been conducted in NSCLC, CRC, and PDAC patients in the second-line or later setting, with these patients having received prior chemotherapy. Experience with other targeted therapies in NSCLC, such as EGFR, ALK, and ROS1 inhibitors, suggests much greater efficacy when used in the first-line setting rather than as later lines of therapy. Similarly, early preclinical and clinical data suggest RAS inhibitors may have greater efficacy in earlier lines of therapy, which may reflect increasing genetic and non-genetic heterogeneity of tumors with subsequent lines of treatment or potentially cross-resistance between chemotherapy and targeted therapy (64,65). For example, recent data reported from the Phase 1 clinical trial of daraxonrasib in patients with advanced PDAC demonstrated that mPFS was slightly higher for patients treated after one line of prior chemotherapy compared with those treated after two lines of prior chemotherapy (66). These data suggest that clinical benefit for RAS inhibitors across a range of cancer types may be improved for patients in earlier lines of therapy, especially in the first-line setting, and several clinical trials are ongoing or planned to evaluate RAS inhibitor combination strategies as first-line therapy.

In NSCLC, the incorporation of RAS inhibition in the first-line setting will require demonstration of improved efficacy and comparable or improved tolerability compared with standard-of-care options, as has been the case with other targeted therapy first-line successes, including EGFR and ALK inhibitors. Benchmarks of first-line therapy efficacy vary according to molecular subtype of NSCLC. For example, in NSCLC with any level of PD-L1 expression and without sensitizing EGFR or ALK alterations, first-line chemoimmunotherapy yields an ORR of 48% and mPFS of 8.8 months (67). To achieve widespread uptake of first-line RAS inhibition in KRAS-mutant NSCLC, KRAS inhibitors will need to be combinable with immune checkpoint blockade and possibly chemotherapy and will need to demonstrate superiority to relevant standards-of-care. Several ongoing randomized trials are investigating the added benefit of KRASG12C inhibitors in first-line advanced NSCLC.

In PDAC, first-line combination chemotherapy regimens yield responses in approximately 30% of patients and a mPFS of about 6 months, often at the expense of considerable toxicity from multiagent therapies (68,69). Thus, the bar may be lower for adoption of safe and effective RAS inhibitor monotherapy or combination regimens in PDAC. Moreover, given that RAS inhibition with mutant-selective, pan-KRAS, or pan-RAS inhibitors may have improved tolerability over some first-line multiagent chemotherapy regimens, RAS inhibitor monotherapy may offer an attractive first-line option for many patients who are too ill at presentation to receive multiagent chemotherapy.

Lastly, the promising early data described above for RAS inhibition in the metastatic setting suggest that moving RAS inhibitors to the neoadjuvant (pre-surgical) or adjuvant (post-surgical) setting will also prove beneficial to patients and potentially enhance the cure rate for resectable KRAS-mutant tumors. This has been demonstrated for other targeted therapies in NSCLC, including EGFR and ALK inhibitors, both of which significantly increase disease-free survival versus chemotherapy in the adjuvant setting (70,71). A similar approach could be envisioned in GI malignancies. For example, in borderline resectable or locally advanced PDAC, surgical resection can be complicated by involvement of key blood vessels surrounding the tumor. These patients receive neoadjuvant chemotherapy, in the hope of reducing vasculature involvement and permitting surgery (72). However, neoadjuvant chemotherapy is ineffective in far too many patients and frequently does not lead to sufficient primary tumor responses to permit surgical resection and potential cure. KRAS inhibitors alone or in combination may provide an additional well-tolerated and effective therapeutic option to enable more patients to receive potentially curative surgery. That said, even with complete surgical resection of primary PDAC tumors, the relapse rate is unacceptably high (73), and adjuvant RAS inhibition in combination with or following neoadjuvant/adjuvant chemotherapy holds great promise to improve relapse rates and long-term disease control. Given the potential for well-tolerated RAS inhibitor-based therapies to improve cure rates when used with standard chemotherapy, radiation, and surgical options, it is likely that RAS inhibitors will eventually advance to become an important component of neoadjuvant and/or adjuvant therapy regimens.

### RAS inhibitor resistance in preclinical and clinical studies

While KRASG12C inhibitors have shown promising efficacy in KRAS-mutant tumors, including NSCLC, CRC, and PDAC, most patients ultimately develop resistance, emphasizing the need for improved treatment and combination strategies. Resistance can be categorized in two major classes: (1) primary resistance, whereby tumors continue to grow despite therapy due to preexisting genetic, transcriptomic, and/or other factors promoting insensitivity to RAS inhibition; and (2) acquired resistance, whereby treatment initially leads to either significant tumor shrinkage or stability, but the tumor eventually resumes growth despite drug treatment due to the acquisition of new genetic or non-genetic resistance mechanisms. To date, several studies have elucidated mechanisms of primary and acquired resistance to KRAS inhibition in patients treated with KRASG12C inhibitors, including sotorasib, adagrasib, and divarasib, across multiple cancer types (Supplemental Table 1) (10–16,32).

For the most part, these studies have assessed circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) before KRAS inhibitor treatment and at the time of acquired resistance to therapy, providing a valuable, though limited, window into potential genetic causes of resistance. Importantly, ctDNA studies have multiple technical limitations, including a restricted number of genes assayed and limitations on sensitivity of detection due to variability in tumor shedding of ctDNA; moreover, they do not provide any insight into transcriptomic or other non-genetic factors leading to resistance. Furthermore, approximately 40% of patients with acquired resistance do not have detectable genetic alterations by ctDNA profiling, thus suggesting that non-genetic mechanisms of resistance, such as adaptive signaling changes, metabolic alterations, or transcriptomic cell state changes may drive resistance.

Very few studies have analyzed on- or post-treatment tumor biopsies, thus limiting the ability to assess the true rates of both genetic and non-genetic drivers contributing to clinical resistance to KRAS inhibition. Given the heterogeneous evolution of resistance in many patients, it is highly likely that both genetic and non-genetic drivers of resistance co-evolve in the same patient during treatment.

#### Primary resistance to KRAS inhibition

Disease control rates (DCR)—defined as CR + PR + SD—in clinical trials of patients treated with KRASG12C inhibitors have generally been high, consistently ranging 80–90% across cancer types, including NSCLC, CRC and PDAC. Conversely, approximately 10–20% of patients across studies demonstrate primary resistance and have PD as best response on therapy, without achieving any clinical benefit. The mechanisms underlying primary resistance to RAS inhibition remain an area of active investigation. In NSCLC, co-occurring genetic alterations that drive inferior outcomes with KRASG12C inhibition have been studied, with mutations in KEAP1 having been consistently associated with lower response rates (17,18,74–76), an observation consistent with prior preclinical data suggesting that KEAP1 alterations can drive resistance to RTK-RAS-MAPK pathway inhibition (77). In line with these findings, transcriptomic analysis of pre-treatment tumors from patients treated with adagrasib has revealed that elevated NRF2-driven antioxidant response gene expression is also associated with worse clinical outcomes to adagrasib monotherapy (76). Genetic co-alterations in KEAP1, SMARCA4, and CDKN2A have been independently associated with early disease progression (PFS ≤ 3 months) and poor clinical outcomes with KRASG12C inhibitor monotherapy (75). Exploratory analyses in KRASG12C lung cancer have also suggested that alterations in the PI3K-AKT-MTOR pathway or additional baseline RAS gene alterations, such as amplifications, may also associate with poorer clinical outcomes (75). Recent work also suggests that NSCLC tumors with higher expression of a squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) signature at baseline correlate with poor adagrasib response in patients with KRAS/LKB1-mutant NSCLC (78).

Studies dissecting mechanisms of primary resistance to KRASG12C inhibition in other tumor types, such as CRC or PDAC, have been more limited, due in part to the lower prevalence of KRASG12C mutations in these cancer types and thus lower numbers of patients for correlative analyses. Adaptive signaling in CRC likely plays a role in driving upfront resistance in a subset of patients, as demonstrated by preclinical and clinical data supporting improved response rates and DCR with the combination of KRAS inhibition and anti-EGFR blockade. The role of frequently co-occurring baseline mutational patterns in CRC (e.g., APC, TP53, SMAD4) and PDAC (e.g., TP53, CDKN2A, SMAD4, ARID1A) or for baseline transcriptional subtypes in driving response or resistance remains an active area of investigation in preclinical models and clinical samples. Recent work assessing ctDNA data from two large cohorts of patients with CRC and PDAC identified candidate primary resistance mutations in ~50% of KRASG12C CRC and ~25% of KRASG12C PDAC (79). These co-occurring baseline mutations in KRASG12C tumors included KRAS, NRAS, and BRAF alterations, EGFR amplification, and mutations in the PI3K pathway, among others. As larger trials of mutant-selective, pan-KRAS, and pan-RAS inhibitors in these disease types mature over the next several years, larger correlative analyses will likely reveal additional genetic and non-genetic modifiers of KRAS inhibitor response.

#### Acquired resistance to KRAS inhibition

Several studies have investigated mechanisms of acquired resistance, with genomic profiling and clinical data now reported from over 200 patients who developed therapeutic resistance after SD or PRs to KRASG12C inhibitors, with most of these patients having NSCLC, CRC, or PDAC (Supplemental Table 1). A putative mechanism of resistance was identified in roughly 60% of these patients, while no etiology of resistance was identified for the remaining patients (Figure 2A–C). Interestingly, while patients with NSCLC or PDAC generally had one or a few putative resistance alterations, multiple potential resistance mechanisms could often be identified in patients with CRC (Figure 2D) (10,11,14,15,32). This finding was even more pronounced in a cohort of CRC patients treated with combination KRAS/EGFR therapy, in which all patients developed multiple treatment-emergent mutations, with as many as 34 new mutations identified in a single patient after treatment (16). In addition to putative genetic etiologies of resistance, several studies have suggested non-genetic mechanisms, including histologic transformation and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), as mediators of clinical resistance.

Because other mutant-selective, pan-KRAS or pan-RAS inhibitors are currently in early phase clinical trials, scant data on resistance mechanisms to these inhibitors has been reported. Thus, resistance data with KRASG12C inhibitors serve as valuable proof-of-concept for putative mechanisms of resistance that will likely be relevant to a wide array of different KRAS inhibitors. Genetic and non-genetic mechanisms of acquired resistance to RAS inhibition and the preclinical and clinical evidence supporting each mechanism are reviewed in detail below.

#### KRAS mutation or amplification

Secondary alterations in KRAS are the most commonly identified resistance mechanisms in genomic data from patients. Mutations in the switch II binding pocket of KRAS, such as R68S, H95D/Q/R, and Y96C, can prevent drug binding while maintaining oncogenic KRAS activity (80). Crystallographic and functional studies have shown that several switch II pocket mutations confer resistance to both sotorasib and adagrasib, while others can differentiate between the compounds (11). Importantly, in preclinical models, KRASG12C (ON) inhibition through a distinct tri-complex mechanism has been shown to effectively overcome switch II pocket mutation (81). In addition to binding pocket alterations, different mutant alleles of KRAS (e.g., G12D, G12V) without the reactive mutant cysteine required for binding can mediate resistance to covalent KRASG12C inhibitors. Multiple preclinical studies employing deep mutational scanning have revealed the comprehensive landscape of secondary mutations that can confer resistance to KRASG12C inhibitors, thus serving as a valuable reference for clinical interpretation (11,40,82). Finally, amplification of KRAS is frequently seen as a resistance mechanism, with amplification of typically the mutant allele but sometimes the WT allele seen in clinical samples. Overexpression of mutant KRAS may overcome available concentrations of KRAS inhibitor. Additionally, overexpression of WT RAS will not be affected by mutant-specific inhibitors (83). Notably, KRAS amplification has been seen repeatedly as a mechanism of acquired resistance in both in vitro and in vivo studies (13,16,57).

#### RTK-RAS-MAPK activation

Activating mutations in the RTK-RAS-MAPK pathway are also common, leading to reactivation of RAS-MAPK signaling despite inhibition of mutant KRAS (Figure 2B–C, Supplemental Table 1). Besides alterations in KRAS itself, BRAF, MAP2K1, and NRAS are among the most commonly mutated genes in the pathway. Alterations in the MAPK pathway upstream of KRAS are rarer, though inactivating mutations in NF1 have been reported. Only one gain-of-function mutation has been reported in PTPN11 (SHP2), found in a CRC patient treated with combination KRAS/EGFR treatment and who had 33 other putative resistance mutations identified (16). Alterations further downstream of MAPK signaling, including amplification of CDK4 or CDK6 or loss-of-function mutations in RB1, have also been observed. Multiple preclinical studies have validated MAPK pathway alterations as drivers of KRAS inhibitor resistance.

Activating alterations in upstream receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) are also commonly found, including activating SNPs (EGFRT790M) or, more commonly, RTK amplification (EGFR, ERBB2, FGFR2, MET, NTRK1). RTK activation can lead to reactivation of MAPK and PI3K pathway signaling despite KRAS inhibition by activating WT KRAS or RAS isoform signaling (84). Notably, among patients with only one putative resistance mechanism identified, MET amplification is the most commonly reported RTK alteration (Supplemental Table 1); this mirrors clinical evidence for other targeted therapies, such as EGFR inhibition, for which MET amplification is a common resistance mechanism in both NSCLC and CRC (85,86). Interestingly, in preclinical studies, overexpression of RTKs in NSCLC and PDAC cell lines led to resistance to adagrasib but not to the pan-RAS inhibitor RMC-7977, suggesting that activation of WT RAS signaling (which would be blocked by a pan-RAS inhibitor) may be a significant component of RTK-mediated resistance (50). A separate study suggested that RTKs promote KRAS inhibitor resistance via IRE1ɑ activation, downstream of a wide range of RTKs, thereby activating the unfolded protein response to promote cell survival despite RAS inhibition (87). Additionally, ERBB2 amplification has been shown to cause KRAS localization to the cytoplasm, with subsequent loss of dependence on KRAS and resistance to KRAS inhibitors (88). Given these disparate reported mechanisms, further characterization is needed to understand RTK-mediated contributions to resistance.

#### PI3K activation

In addition to upstream RTK activation of the PI3K pathway, alterations in the PI3K pathway itself are also seen in patients with acquired resistance. These include both activating mutations in PIK3CA and inactivating mutations in PTEN. The PI3K pathway is both downstream of RAS and RTK signaling and serves as an alternative mechanism of cell growth and proliferation to the MAPK pathway, and constitutive activation is known to promote oncogenesis in its own right (89).

These clinical findings mirror preclinical studies, in which PI3K signaling contributes to both primary and acquired resistance. In one study, the LU99 NSCLC cell line, which has activating mutations in both KRAS and PIK3CA, was found to have primary resistance to sotorasib, while two KRAS-mutant cell lines that developed resistance to sotorasib after several months of treatment demonstrated constitutive activation of the PI3K pathway (90). Similarly, in a panel of 20 KRASG12D PDAC patient-derived organoids treated with MRTX1133, the second-most resistant model harbored an activating mutation in PIK3CA (13). Importantly, co-mutation of KRAS and PI3K pathway members in untreated patients is not uncommon; in CRC, KRAS/PI3K pathway co-mutation has been reported in 8.4% of patients (91), and in PDAC, KRAS/PI3K pathway co-mutation has been reported in 3–10% of patients (92,93), suggesting sizeable subsets of patients who may have some degree of primary resistance to KRAS inhibitors due to PI3K pathway activation. Additional preclinical and clinical studies are necessary to characterize the contributions of PI3K mutations to both primary and acquired KRAS inhibitor resistance.

#### MYC amplification

MYC signaling constitutes another growth pathway found to have association with both primary and acquired resistance via MYC amplification. Similar to the PI3K activation, MYC activation is downstream of many key signaling pathways, and MYC amplification is known to promote oncogenesis. Multiple preclinical studies have identified MYC signaling as a resistance mechanism for KRAS inhibitors (13,94). One study treated mice with KRAS-mutant pancreatic tumors with the pan-RAS inhibitor RMC-7977, finding that nearly 2/3 of mice with acquired resistance had developed MYC copy number gains; subsequent mechanistic studies suggested that MYC activation led to KRAS inhibitor resistance, at least in part, via activation of YAP/TAZ signaling (53).

#### TP53 mutation

The p53 tumor suppressor plays a crucial role in regulating cell division and triggering apoptosis in response to cellular stresses such as DNA damage. Inactivating mutations in TP53 are a common cause of drug resistance across many cancer therapeutics. Acquired TP53 mutations have been observed in ctDNA data upon resistance to KRAS inhibitors, although whether these TP53 mutations are truly acquired during treatment and represent true drivers of resistance remains to be confirmed. Importantly, co-mutation of KRAS and TP53 is common, with up to 50% of KRAS-mutant NSCLC and CRC harboring TP53 mutations (95,96), and up to 70% of KRAS-mutant PDAC harboring TP53 mutations (97). As such, TP53 mutation may also contribute to primary resistance to KRAS inhibitors. Different TP53 mutations confer different levels of gene inactivation (98). Substantially more preclinical studies and clinical data will be needed to firmly establish the relationship between TP53 mutations and acquired or primary resistance.

#### Histologic transformation and cell state changes

Mounting evidence in preclinical models and clinical samples suggests that histologic and transcriptomic changes in cancer cell state may drive resistance to KRAS inhibition (Figure 3A–B). In lung adenocarcinoma, histologic transformation consistent with transdifferentiation to or selection for other lung cancer cell types has been observed in response to KRAS inhibition, similar to prior studies showing histologic changes at resistance to other targeted therapies, including EGFR inhibitors (99). Preclinical studies using KRASG12D lung cancer mouse models have demonstrated that treatment with KRAS inhibitors induced differentiation of lung adenocarcinoma cells to an alveolar type-1-like state, conferring resistance (100). In two patients with NSCLC, histologic transformation from adenocarcinoma to squamous cell carcinoma was observed without identification of concurrent acquired genetic alterations (11). Adenocarcinoma to squamous cell carcinoma transition (AST) has previously been reported to confer resistance to other targeted therapies in NSCLC (101). Recent work in genetically engineered mouse models (GEMMs) and organoid models of lung adenocarcinoma have demonstrated that AST drives resistance to KRAS inhibition through an ELF5-DNp63 signaling axis (78). Furthermore, a case report of rapid autopsy of a NSCLC patient who developed acquired resistance to sotorasib identified no new oncogenic mutations, but did find activation of mesenchymal signaling, suggesting EMT as a potential transcriptomic etiology of resistance (102). Importantly, assessment for histologic change upon drug resistance is rarely pursued clinically, as it requires pre- and post-treatment biopsies as well as subsequent transcriptomic or immunohistochemical analysis, suggesting that these mechanisms of resistance likely occur more commonly than is currently appreciated.

EMT has long been associated with drug resistance. EMT refers to a change in cell state, in which cells lose epithelial and gain mesenchymal properties, including increased motility, invasive capability, and stemness. As it is driven by epigenetic and transcriptional changes, EMT is reversible, and cancer cells can switch between these states in response to various stimuli, including drug treatment; cancer cells can also occupy an intermediate state, termed partial EMT, with properties of both states (Figure 3A). Many studies have demonstrated that EMT confers both chemoresistance (103,104) and resistance to targeted therapies (105,106), including resistance to KRAS suppression or inhibition (13,107,108). An early study testing sotorasib in a panel of NSCLC cell lines found that EMT correlated with primary resistance and that induction of EMT-associated transcription factors TWIST or SNAIL led to acquired resistance (108). Similarly, proteomics studies demonstrated that induction of EMT, as measured by either EMT-associated surface markers (CDH1, VIM) or protein-set enrichment analysis, correlated with resistance to KRAS inhibitors (109). Moreover, in studies comparing MRTX1133-resistant and MRTX1133-sensitive PDAC cell lines, EMT is the most enriched pathway in the resistant cell lines, and murine and human KRASG12D cell lines treated with increasing doses of MRTX1133 to model acquired resistance demonstrate consistent upregulation of EMT RNA signatures and protein biomarkers with the resistant phenotype (13). As more transcriptomic data from on- and post-treatment biopsy samples become available, we suspect that we will continue to see EMT enriched at drug resistance, either in patients without genetic resistance mechanisms or as a co-evolving mechanism with genetic alterations (Figure 3B).

While EMT has been clearly associated with resistance to KRAS inhibition in preclinical models and some patient samples, recent preclinical studies have suggested additional complexity to the relationship of cell state along the epithelial and mesenchymal axis and KRAS inhibitor resistance, suggesting that certain epithelial or partial EMT states may also drive resistance. Work in PDAC GEMMs demonstrated that early in treatment with KRAS inhibitors, mesenchymal cells or basal-like cells were actually more sensitive than epithelial cell types (13). However, upon progression to resistant tumors, partial EMT and mesenchymal cells comprised the majority of cycling cells (13). Lineage tracing studies in PDAC mouse models identified a subset of epithelial Lgals4+ cells resistant to KRAS inhibition, and these cells served as a reservoir for disease relapse after KRAS treatment (110). Moreover, studies in NSCLC mouse models identified a partial epithelial state, with properties of multiple lung lineage differentiations, which was tolerant to pan-RAS inhibition (111). Taken together, these data suggest that mesenchymal cells may initially be more sensitive to KRAS inhibition, but that the acquisition of additional transcriptomic features ultimately leads to mesenchymal and partial EMT cells causing resistance and disease progression. Better understanding the magnitude and temporal dynamics of transcriptomic shifts that occur after KRAS inhibitor treatment will be key to understanding the contributions of each of these states to resistance.

#### YAP/TAZ/TEAD signaling

An orthogonal transcriptomic alteration associated with KRAS inhibitor resistance is negative regulation of the Hippo signaling pathway, which leads to activation of the transcriptional regulators YAP and TAZ. YAP/TAZ subsequently translocate to the nucleus, where they interact with TEAD family proteins to drive cell proliferation and survival through a variety of downstream signaling pathways, including activation of EMT signaling (112). RAS signaling is known to intersect with the Hippo pathway, and activated RAS proteins interact with RASSF proteins to inhibit Hippo signaling and subsequently activate YAP/TAZ (113). Additionally, YAP/TAZ/TEAD form a complex with AP-1, which is downstream of KRAS/MAPK signaling, to promote growth and proliferation (114). Importantly, multiple preclinical studies have shown that YAP/TAZ signaling contributes to KRAS inhibitor resistance.

More than a decade ago, YAP was shown to rescue growth and viability in KRAS-mutant cells undergoing KRAS suppression (115). Studies using the iKras PDAC GEMM model with inducible suppression of oncogenic KrasG12D expression in established tumors also demonstrated that Yap1 amplification and activation of Yap/Tead signaling can drive Kras-independent tumor growth (116). More recently, KRAS inhibition has been shown to cause mislocalization of the apical-basal polarity protein Scribble, leading to increased YAP signaling and subsequent MRAS activation; MRAS activation bypassed KRAS inhibitor treatment and reactivated MAPK signaling (117). Another study modeled acquired resistance to KRAS inhibition in cell lines via prolonged treatment with sotorasib, showing that the resistant cell lines upregulated YAP/TAZ signaling and had acquired sensitivity to YAP/TAZ inhibition via a pan-TEAD inhibitor as monotherapy or in combination with sotorasib (Figure 3C) (118). Moreover, in the aforementioned GEMM studies of acquired resistance to the pan-RAS inhibitor RMC-7977, Myc activation was proposed to drive KRAS inhibitor resistance, at least in part, through activation of Yap1 signaling (53). Other studies have shown synergy between KRAS and TEAD inhibitors, as well (119). Given the lack of biopsy studies at KRAS inhibitor resistance, there is currently insufficient clinical validation of YAP/TAZ transcriptional activation as a resistance mechanism, and gaining a better understanding of the contribution of this pathway to clinical resistance will be very important, especially as YAP-TEAD inhibitors progress in the clinic.

#### Limitations in current understanding of RAS inhibitor resistance

While multiple putative resistance mechanisms have been identified, several key factors have limited a comprehensive understanding of clinical resistance to RAS inhibitors. The existing genetic studies of acquired resistance were almost all performed with KRASG12C inhibitors; future studies with other mutant-selective, pan-KRAS, or pan-RAS inhibitors will be needed to understand which resistance mechanisms are drug-specific versus those which more generally apply across different RAS inhibitors. Furthermore, most of the data implicating various genetic and non-genetic mechanisms in resistance has been correlative in nature, and rigorous laboratory testing will be needed to demonstrate that each alteration is able to increase resistance to KRAS inhibition in faithful preclinical models. Additional patient-derived and engineered models will be necessary to fully investigate each putative resistance mechanism. While ctDNA studies have implicated many potential acquired genetic alterations at resistance, the variant allele frequency (VAF) for many of these mutations, especially secondary switch II pocket KRAS mutations, is low at the time of detection and can remain low throughout progression of disease (10,11). The full contribution of variants with low VAF to clinical progression of disease compared with other co-evolving genetic and non-genetic mechanisms is unclear and requires further study in laboratory models and in biopsy specimens from patients on clinical trials.

Many genetic resistance mechanisms lead to reactivation of the MAPK pathway or of parallel pathways despite KRAS inhibition. On withdrawal of KRAS inhibitor, KRAS may resume oncogenic signaling, leading to further MAPK activation. Such extreme hyperactivation of these pathways paradoxically can be detrimental to cancer cells, leading to activation lethality and reduced growth or even cell death in certain circumstances (120). This was highlighted in CRC patients treated with EGFR/KRAS combination therapy, for which KRAS amplification was a common resistance mechanism with high VAF while on treatment; however, upon treatment withdrawal, the VAF for KRAS amplification precipitously dropped, suggesting reduced cancer cell proliferation and viability or acquisition of a senescent phenotype in the setting of uninhibited amplified KRAS signaling (16). The same group showed similar results in preclinical studies of KRAS amplification. Importantly, regression of resistant clones by such RAS pathway hyperactivation-induced lethality and other mechanisms, as well as repopulation of the tumor burden by non-resistant clones upon withdrawal of KRAS inhibitor, could ultimately lead to loss of the clinically resistant phenotype, thus allowing for KRAS inhibitor rechallenge in patients. This paradigm was recently demonstrated in a patient with KRASG12C CRC who developed resistance to adagrasib/cetuximab associated with a KRASQ61H resistance mutation, but whose KRASQ61H resistance mutation spontaneously regressed while off of KRASG12C therapy, allowing for successful retreatment with adagrasib/cetuximab (121). Longitudinal ctDNA testing, even after progression and drug withdrawal, will help understand which resistance mutations recede after KRAS inhibitors are withdrawn and will potentially inform when rechallenge with a KRAS inhibitor therapy is warranted.

Lastly, the role of epigenetic, transcriptional, and metabolic changes that drive resistance to RAS inhibition will require biopsy studies to determine the evolution of these features during response and resistance, as well as to identify co-occurring genetic resistance mechanisms. Almost certainly, genetic and non-genetic resistance mechanisms will co-exist in many patients, and the contribution of each to clinical resistance will require experimental studies. Similarly, non-tumor cell intrinsic mechanisms involving intercellular signaling with immune and non-immune (e.g., fibroblasts, endothelial) stromal cells in the tumor microenvironment or tumor cell interactions with the extracellular matrix likely play important roles in mediating signals that may drive resistance. Elucidation of these potential mechanisms of resistance will require serial tumor biopsies during response and resistance and application of single-cell and spatial profiling technologies in a systematic manner.

### Combination therapy with KRAS inhibitors

KRAS inhibitors have demonstrated exciting clinical efficacy to date; however, combination therapy will be necessary to combat resistance mechanisms and to extend the depth and durability of response. The mechanisms of resistance to KRAS inhibitors described above offer initial opportunities for the rational development of combinations to overcome resistance (Figure 4). We can also draw upon lessons learned from past efforts to develop combinations with other targeted therapies.

#### Improving KRAS inhibitor potency to enhance clinical efficacy

KRAS inhibitors with optimal potency and tolerability will be the key foundation for combination therapy strategies. Critically, improvements in KRAS inhibitor efficacy will come from the development of next-generation KRAS inhibitors, with optimized on-target potency and engagement, mirroring experience with prior targeted therapy paradigms. For example, EGFR was one of the first successfully targeted oncogenes, with clinical trials demonstrating the superiority of the EGFR inhibitor gefitinib to chemotherapy in EGFR-mutant NSCLC in 2009 (122). Gefitinib was clearly superior to chemotherapy, with more and deeper clinical responses, but resistance rapidly developed, with a primary mechanism of resistance being the development of the EGFRT790M mutation, which hinders gefitinib binding. Eventually, the third-generation EGFR inhibitor osimertinib was developed to inhibit T790M, and the FLAURA trial demonstrated that first-line osimertinib nearly doubled PFS as compared to first-generation EGFR inhibitors, driven largely by preventing on-target resistance through T790M and other mutations (123). Beyond EGFR, rational design of next-generation inhibitors to address resistance mutations and increase CNS penetration has also led to development of highly effective therapeutics targeting ALK-rearranged NSCLC. For example, the third-generation ALK inhibitor lorlatinib demonstrates PFS >5 years in previously untreated patients with ALK-positive NSCLC (124,125).

Improved ORR and DCR is already being observed in the clinic with next-generation KRASG12C inhibitors, for which preclinical studies have suggested that among KRASG12C inhibitors, divarasib has higher potency than adagrasib, which has higher potency than sotorasib (126). Correspondingly, early phase clinical trials of divarasib have suggested that this agent may yield the greatest clinical efficacy of these three KRASG12C inhibitors, and adagrasib has demonstrated greater response rates than sotorasib in NSCLC, CRC and PDAC. Importantly, however, the response rates of these agents are still more modest than those of other targeted therapies such as EGFR inhibitors (80% ORR for first-line treatment of EGFR-mutant NSCLC (123)), suggesting significant room for further optimization of KRAS inhibitor potency and selectivity, or potentially distinct biology or oncogene dependency between EGFR–mutant and KRAS–mutant NSCLC (such as the fact that EGFR-mutant NSCLC more typically occurs in never-smokers, whereas KRASG12C NSCLC typically arises in patients with a significant smoking history). Multiple mutant-selective, pan-KRAS, and pan-RAS inhibitors are currently in preclinical and clinical development, and novel drug discovery efforts, such as artificial intelligence-based drug design, are also being employed to identify next-generation inhibitors (127). Identification of those agents with maximal ability to inhibit oncogenic KRAS signaling at tolerable dosing will be critical to establishing the optimal backbone for multiple combination therapy strategies.

#### Combinations targeting RAS

Similar to the experience with EGFR, alterations in KRAS are the most commonly seen alterations in patients with acquired resistance—these alterations include mutations causing steric hindrance with particular KRAS inhibitors, secondary activating mutations in KRAS, and amplification of the mutant or WT KRAS allele (Figure 2B–C) (11,13,16,80). Combination therapy targeted at KRAS itself therefore may consist of KRAS inhibitors targeting different mutant and WT alleles of KRAS. This therapeutic concept is already being tested in early clinical trials with the addition of the pan-RAS inhibitor daraxonrasib to the mutant-selective KRAS (ON) inhibitors elironrasib or zoldonrasib. In this strategy, the mutant-selective KRAS (ON) inhibitor inhibits the original KRAS mutation, while daraxonrasib may be able to inhibit both WT RAS proteins and novel treatment-emergent mutant isoforms of RAS, preventing the development of RAS-mediated resistance. Preliminary data from the daraxonrasib/elironrasib combination have suggested greater efficacy in CRC from the combination than from either drug alone but with greater toxicity (55); ongoing clinical trials will inform whether this approach is tolerable and leads to deeper and or longer responses. Another potential opportunity includes combining RAS inhibitors with different MOAs, in order to maximally suppress KRAS signaling. These could include combining KRAS (OFF) and KRAS (ON) inhibitors or combining RAS inhibitors with RAS degraders.

#### Vertical pathway inhibition

Combination therapy strategies targeting multiple nodes in the RTK-RAS-MAPK pathway have been critical to the success of BRAF-targeted therapy in various cancer types, including melanoma and CRC. Such vertical pathway inhibition seeks to maximally suppress oncogenic signaling while blocking adaptive feedback signals that may mediate resistance. BRAF inhibitors were first approved in BRAF-mutant melanoma in 2011, after the BRIM3 trial demonstrated clear benefit of the BRAFV600E inhibitor vemurafenib over single agent chemotherapy (128). In order to improve efficacy and also address paradoxical activation leading to secondary skin cancers, BRAF inhibitors were combined with MEK inhibitors, which also had shown modest single agent activity in BRAF-mutant tumors (129). The combination of the mutant-selective BRAF inhibitor dabrafenib and the MEK1/2 inhibitor trametinib in melanoma demonstrated significantly increased survival versus dabrafenib alone (130). The combination of BRAF inhibition and MEK inhibition is now approved in a tissue-agnostic manner for adult and pediatric tumors harboring a BRAFV600E mutation. While efficacious in melanoma, single agent vemurafenib had limited efficacy in other BRAF-mutant tumors such as CRC (131), and the addition of MEK inhibitors to BRAF therapy did not substantially increase efficacy. As noted above, EGFR signaling had been reported to be a driver of CRC resistance to BRAF therapy in preclinical studies, and anti-EGFR antibodies were added to the BRAF inhibition in clinical trials. This led to substantially increased efficacy in CRC, and doublet combination therapy with BRAF inhibition and anti-EGFR antibodies is now standard-of-care for BRAF-mutant CRC (26,28). Similarly, activation of other RTKs such as MET and HER2 is commonly found to confer resistance to EGFR TKIs in EGFR-mutant NSCLC through reactivation of the MAPK and PI3K growth pathways. MET amplification, especially, has been associated with resistance, and MET inhibitors have been successfully combined with osimertinib to overcome MET amplification-induced resistance to osimertinib in multiple trials, though overall response rates and durations of response have been somewhat modest (132,133). Genomic heterogeneity of MET amplification and/or lack of a high degree of oncogene dependency associated with MET amplification may explain why targeting MET-driven resistance does not lead to more durable efficacy. Furthermore, the METxEGFR bispecific antibody amivantamab is approved in combination with the EGFR inhibitor lazertinib for first-line treatment of EGFR-mutant NSCLC, where the combination demonstrated a ~7 month increased PFS versus osimertinib and a statistically significant improvement in overall survival expected to be >12 months; importantly, this approach successfully added MET inhibition upfront to prevent resistance, rather than treating at the time of MET-mediated resistance (134,135). Given the success of these paradigms for BRAF and EGFR-targeted therapies, vertical combination therapy strategies for KRAS-mutant tumors through targeting multiple nodes in the RTK-RAS pathway are actively being investigated.

#### RTKs

Combination strategies targeting upstream RTKs with KRAS inhibition have been extensively evaluated in preclinical studies and clinical trials. Such approaches aim both to further reduce active RAS signaling and to inhibit bypass signaling pathways through WT RAS and PI3K pathways. As noted above, clinical trials have demonstrated efficacy of KRASG12C inhibition in combination with anti-EGFR antibodies in CRC, mirroring clinical experience with BRAF inhibitors and leading to the first approved combinations with KRAS inhibition. The success of combining KRAS and EGFR inhibition in CRC suggests that combining KRAS inhibitors with other RTK inhibitors may work as well. Other tumor types may rely on differing RTK signaling pathways for growth and/or resistance; such lineage-specific RTK signaling could be intrinsic to tumor cells or influenced by lineage-specific tumor microenvironments, such as stroma-induced FGFR signaling in PDAC (136). In NSCLC, prior experience adding MET inhibition in EGFR-mutant NSCLC would suggest that MET inhibitors may similarly be good combination partners with KRAS inhibitors.

Separately, amplification of several RTKs has been found in patients with acquired resistance, including EGFR, ERBB2, FGFR2, and MET, among others. Small molecule and/or antibody inhibitors are available and approved for each of these RTKs, and in the setting of acquired resistance due to an RTK amplification, adding the appropriate anti-RTK agent to KRAS inhibition could overcome resistance, though durability of responses may be limited, as noted above for targeting MET amplification-driven resistance in EGFR-mutant NSCLC. Appropriately designed clinical trials of these combination approaches will need to be conducted.

#### SHP2 and SOS1

Downstream of RTKs but still upstream of RAS are SHP2 and SOS1, both of which are crucial in RAS pathway signaling. SOS1 acts as a GEF for RAS, exchanging GDP for GTP leading to KRAS activation, and SHP2 facilitates colocalization of SOS1 and KRAS. Small molecule inhibitors have been developed for both SHP2 and SOS1, and preclinical studies have suggested that combining SHP2 or SOS1 inhibitors with KRAS inhibitors may further reduce KRAS signaling (137,138). Several clinical trials combining KRAS and SHP2 inhibitors are underway, with some evidence of promising preliminary efficacy (139,140), although the tolerability of these combinations remains a major concern. Optimization of alternative dosing schedules for concurrent administration of KRAS and SHP2 inhibitors will likely be necessary to mitigate toxicity from this combination. KRAS and SOS1 inhibitor combinations are also under active investigation.

#### MEK and ERK

Combination approaches targeting downstream inhibitors of MAPK signaling nodes, including MEK1/2 and ERK1/2, may aid in maximally suppressing the RAS-MAPK pathway; however, these combinations may be limited by toxicity due to non-selective inhibition of MAPK signaling in both tumor and normal cells. For instance, in a trial combining sotorasib with the MEK1/2 inhibitor trametinib, 24% of patients had to discontinue one or both of the drugs due to toxicity from the combination (141). Activating mutations in BRAF and MEK1 have been identified in patients with acquired resistance to KRAS inhibitors, and these tumors may demonstrate enhanced responses to the addition of targeted therapy against those alterations, including BRAFV600E or MEK1/2 inhibitors. Multiple clinical trials are ongoing investigating these concepts.

#### PI3K pathway

Activation of the PI3K pathway is commonly seen in acquired resistance to KRAS inhibitors, including by adaptive signaling mechanisms, as well as through activating mutations in PIK3CA or by inactivating mutations in PTEN. For patients who develop PIK3CA mutations, approved pan-PIK3CA inhibitors could be appropriate KRAS combination partners. Notably, the majority of PIK3CA mutations observed in KRAS acquired resistance are at the E542, E545, and H1047 hotspots (Supplemental Table 1), and mutant-selective PIK3CA inhibitors able to selectively inhibit all of these mutations are under clinical development (142–144). The combination of mutant-selective KRAS and mutant-selective PIK3CA inhibitors would be expected to have reduced toxicity versus combinations with pan-inhibitors, given the tumor selectivity of both agents. Moreover, for patients with PI3K pathway activation driving resistance, further downstream inhibitors could be added to treatment, such as the recently-approved pan-AKT inhibitor capivasertib (145) or MTOR inhibitors.

#### YAP/TAZ-TEAD inhibition

The Hippo and YAP/TAZ/TEAD signaling pathway has been extensively associated with preclinical KRAS inhibitor resistance, as noted above. Negative regulation of the Hippo pathway leads to nuclear localization of the transcriptional co-activators YAP/TAZ, which require binding to TEAD transcription factors for signaling activation. There are four TEAD paralogs (TEAD1–4), with partially overlapping pathway activation for each paralog. TEAD selective and pan-TEAD inhibitors have been reported, and both TEAD1 and pan-TEAD inhibitors have been shown to synergize with KRAS inhibitors in preclinical studies (118,146). In vivo studies with the pan-TEAD inhibitor VT-104 showed no tumor growth inhibition with VT-104 as monotherapy, but demonstrated synergistic growth inhibition in combination with adagrasib in KRASG12C CRC (146). Similarly, in vivo studies with the pan-TEAD inhibitor GNE-7883 showed limited efficacy as monotherapy in a sotorasib-resistant KRASG12C NSCLC model; however, combining GNE-7883 with sotorasib was highly effective and prevented tumor growth (118). Preliminary clinical efficacy has been seen for TEAD inhibitors in tumors for which dysregulated Hippo signaling is the oncogenic driver, such as mesothelioma (147); however, clinical trials combining these agents with targeted therapy as a mechanism for overcoming transcriptional drug resistance are currently still underway. Interestingly, YAP/TAZ signaling has been reported to activate EMT (148), so signaling inhibition of this pathway via TEAD inhibition or other mechanisms may block both of these transcriptional pathways associated with KRAS inhibitor resistance.

#### Cell state inhibition

As noted above, nearly 40% of patients do not have putative resistance mechanisms identified via ctDNA testing, suggesting the possibility that epigenetic and transcriptional changes are contributing to resistance. Therapeutic targeting of drug-resistant cell states represents an attractive therapeutic strategy to sensitize cancer cells to KRAS inhibition. Such sensitization to KRAS inhibitors could be achieved via multiple related mechanisms, including through the induction of KRAS inhibitor-sensitive states or inhibition of progression into KRAS inhibitor-resistant states. A complementary approach is to identify drugs able to kill KRAS inhibitor-resistant cell states outright, rather than shifting cells into KRAS inhibitor-sensitive states (Figure 3C). Importantly, cell state inhibitors would theoretically be less likely to work as single-agent therapies and instead would be most effective in combination. Thus, advancing cell state-targeting therapeutics to clinical utility may require industry drug developers and regulatory bodies to embrace upfront evaluation of safety and efficacy in rationally designed combinations, rather than requiring demonstration of monotherapy efficacy as a prerequisite to move toward combination therapy.

#### EMT

Inhibiting EMT has been a therapeutic goal for decades, with many efforts being made to block TGF-β signaling, one of the most well-described mechanisms of EMT activation. Several TGF-β receptor small molecule inhibitors and anti-TGF-β antibodies/ligands have advanced to clinical trials; however, most have been tested as monotherapies, with none currently approved (149,150). Combining these inhibitors with KRAS inhibitors could prevent EMT-induced KRAS resistance, although the safety of targeting the TGF-β pathway remains in question. Other than direct TGF-β signaling inhibitors, a wide range of other transcriptional modulators have been reported to inhibit EMT signaling, notably including FDA-approved drugs such as epigenetic modulators like histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitors (151) and the angiotensin II receptor blocker losartan, commonly used for hypertension (152,153). The actual contributions of each of these drugs to EMT inhibition and their subsequent combinatorial activity with KRAS inhibitors would need to be confirmed and validated prior to embarking on clinical studies; however, the fact that they are already approved would facilitate rapid progression to combination clinical studies.

While EMT is classically driven via TGF-ß signaling and through the activation of ZEB1, TWIST, and SNAIL transcription factor signaling, many differing pathways have been reported to activate EMT and, separately, to maintain mesenchymal signaling. At present, it is not clear which of these pathways are necessary or sufficient for the development of KRAS inhibitor resistance. Further mechanistic understanding of epithelial, mesenchymal, and intermediate cell programs is needed to guide future combination therapy strategies.

#### Orthogonal combination therapy mechanisms

While the above approaches have focused on combinations targeting putative resistance mechanisms, traditional drug combinations involving chemotherapy or immunotherapy have sound scientific rationale and clinical precedent and are being actively pursued. Such combinations may work by orthogonal mechanisms of anti-tumor activity compared to KRAS inhibitors, such that tumor cells would need to develop resistance to each orthogonal mechanism simultaneously. An important consideration for these combinations is that first-line treatment for many tumor types, including KRAS-mutant NSCLC, CRC, and PDAC, consists of chemotherapy and/or immunotherapy. As such, combining KRAS inhibitors with these agents will likely be important to advance KRAS inhibitors to earlier lines of therapy.

#### Chemotherapy

Multiagent chemotherapy regimens are cornerstones of treatment of NSCLC, CRC, and PDAC. The chemotherapies used in these regimens are generally cytotoxic, with activity against rapidly growing cells, but without further selectivity for tumor cells. As such, they have significant toxicities, which can limit the ability to further combine drugs with them. That said, there are many examples of combinations of targeted therapies and chemotherapies with efficacy and tolerability in the clinic. In first-line treatment of EGFR-mutant NSCLC, adding multiagent chemotherapy to the EGFR inhibitor osimertinib led to more durable responses compared with osimertinib alone, at the cost of increased toxicity from the combination. Overall survival data are immature, but there was also a trend toward increased survival in the combination arm (154). Similarly, adding the BRAFV600E inhibitor encorafenib and the anti-EGFR antibody cetuximab to multiagent chemotherapy led to significantly increased response rate and a preliminary trend towards increased overall survival over chemotherapy alone in the first-line treatment of BRAF-mutant CRC (155). These results suggest that combining KRAS inhibition with multiagent chemotherapy may be beneficial as well.

Indeed, preclinical studies have shown combinatorial cell killing with the addition of chemotherapy to KRAS inhibition in PDAC mouse models (13,110), in part through targeting distinct cancer cell states with differential sensitivity to chemotherapy or KRAS inhibitors. There are several ongoing clinical trials adding KRAS inhibitors to chemotherapy regimens in both first and subsequent lines of therapy in multiple tumor types. The therapeutic index of mutant-selective KRAS inhibitors should enable tolerable combinations with chemotherapy, and ongoing and future clinical trials will investigate the efficacy of such combinations across a range of cancer types. Importantly, given the baseline toxicity of chemotherapy regimens, it remains to be seen which chemotherapy regimens can be safely combined with pan-(K)RAS inhibitors that also target WT RAS isoforms. The tolerability of these combinations will likely be influenced by overlapping toxicities of the specific chemotherapy regimens. For example, overlapping GI toxicity between RAS inhibitors and certain chemotherapies, such as irinotecan, may complicate administration of such combination regimens to patients. Ultimately, the best combination chemotherapy agents with mutant-selective or pan-(K)RAS inhibitors and the dose and schedule of administration will need to be evaluated in clinical trials, balancing improved efficacy with tolerability.

#### ADCs

Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) are a novel therapeutic modality seeking to target chemotherapy specifically to tumor cells. Antibodies against tumor antigens are used to bring chemotherapy payloads to tumor cells, thereby reducing systemic chemotherapy exposure and widening the therapeutic window.
