### METHOD DETAILS

#### Identification of PDAC-associated dependencies

Genome-wide CRISPR dependency effect sizes were obtained from the DepMap 24Q2 Chronos dataset. These data are publicly available through the DepMap portal. These dependency effect sizes are quantified as Chronos scores, a statistical measure inferred from a population dynamics model that corrects for sgRNA efficacy, screen quality and cell intrinsic growth rates, and bias related to DNA cutting toxicity. 45 Dependency scores are continuous values that range in magnitude but have empirically demonstrated that essential genes commonly have Chronos score < − 1, and unexpressed genes commonly have Chronos score equal to 0. We thus defined a threshold of Chronos score < − 0.5 as a cutoff to classify gene dependencies for our various analyses. A threshold of − 0.5 strikes a balance by capturing genes with meaningful functional impact on cell survival or proliferation, while reducing the risk of false positives from minor fitness effects. 104

We categorized dependencies in PDAC, by first defining recurrent PDAC dependencies among the 45 PDAC cell line profiled in DepMap. A threshold of dependency in at least 5 PDAC cell lines, was used to define recurrent dependencies. This approximates the proportion (e.g., 10%) comparable to that for major molecular subtypes of other cancers such as triple negative breast cancer.43 ,44 While somewhat arbitrary, this reflects a compromise between stringency and inclusiveness: it avoids limiting our analysis only to pan-essential genes (which are less likely to offer tumor selectivity), while still focusing on targets with reproducible dependencies across multiple models, and enough patients to justify a therapeutic development campaign. This approach identified 2185 recurrent PDAC dependencies. We further defined two subgroups within recurrent PDAC dependencies: Clinically Tractable and PDAC Selective. Data for clinical tractability was obtained from OpenTargets. A target was considered clinically tractable if a targeting compound was classified as in the “Advanced Clinical” or “Approved Drug” category. 46 Subunit proteins where multiple subunit members were strongly dependent (median Chronos score < − 1) across PDAC lines were excluded from analyses. Targeting compounds for subunit protein complexes were annotated as specific for all subunit members, and due to the large number of subunit proteins and their frequent essentiality, we removed them. PDAC-selective dependencies were nominated by a skewed likelihood ratio test (LRT), and those which contained a skewed LRT metric of greater than 100 were identified as being ‘strongly selective.’ In brief, the LRT metric is defined as twice the log of the likelihood ratio of a fitted skewed distribution of gene sensitivity (across all lineages) over the likelihood of a fitted normal distribution. 29 Notably, these criteria may not identify essential genes with biomarker relationships observed in other cancer types but not PDAC, e.g., BRAF dependency in BRAF-mutant cancer types. 47 However, such dependencies with therapeutic implications may also be captured in the class of clinically tractable dependencies.

Dependencies were further evaluated for PDAC enrichment by a two-sided Mann-Whitney U test between gene dependency Chronos scores in PDAC vs. non-PDAC cell lines, with a cutoff q value of <0.01 used to classify enrichment. Genes with a negative U-statistic were considered to exhibit stronger dependencies in PDAC relative to non-PDAC lines. p-values were adjusted to account for false discovery rate. Enrichment scores are reported as the -Log10 of the adjusted p-values. To analyze gene set terms associated with PDAC selective genes, we performed an over representation analysis using the g:Profiler web server (https://biit.cs.ut.ee/gprofiler/gost). Gene sets with less than 500 genes were included for analysis, and statistically significant signatures at an FDR-adjusted p-value of less than 0.01 were plotted.

#### Biomarkers of PDAC-associated dependencies

Biomarkers associated with dependencies were identified by Pearson correlation coefficients as well as the relative importance of the predictive feature, as detailed by DepMap. 32 In brief, the relative importance is a statistic derived from random forest machine learning models that are built individually for each gene dependency. The relative importance is a continuous value ranging from 0 to 1 that indicates the impact of the feature on prediction accuracy relative to other features in the model. It is computed with Gini importance and is normalized so that the sum of all feature importances add up to 1. Higher feature importance denotes an increased ability to predict dependency from that biomarker. Methods for quantification of biomarkers are detailed by DepMap elsewhere.80 In brief, gene expression levels were quantified as log2 (TPM+1) and gene copy number was computed relative to the ploidy of the rest of the genome for a given cell line. Mutations and chromosomal aberrations were identified using SNP array chips. RNA expression, copy number, and chromosomal aberration data was retrieved from the 24Q2 DepMap release.

#### Gene dependencies associated with common genetic alterations

We sought to identify dependencies associated with common genetic alterations in PDAC (KRAS mutation, TP53 mutation, SMAD4 copy number alteration or mutation, and CDKN2A copy number alteration or mutation. For binary mutation variables, we calculated a moderated effect size statistic using the two-class comparison tool in the DepMap analysis portal. This statistic represents the difference in mean value between two groups (i.e., mutant vs. WT across all 1150 CCLE cell lines), with statistical significance assessed using an empirical Bayes approach using the adaptive shrinkage method. This is implemented in the ‘ashr’ CRAN package. For SMAD4 and CDKN2A copy number alteration, we computed the Pearson correlation coefficient between gene dependency Chronos scores and gene copy number for PDAC lines and CCLE cell lines separately.

#### Gene dependencies associated with transcriptional state

To identify dependencies that may be specifically associated with the classical and basal-like states, 55 we computed scores of the Moffitt classical and basal-like signatures 55 using single sample gene set enrichment analyses (ssGSEA). 105 These relationships were computed using gene expression data of PDAC cell lines. To assess genetic dependencies associated with the basal and classical transcriptional states, we performed a two-class comparison in the DepMap analysis portal comparing the top and bottom quartile of signature score across PDAC cell lines for each of the basal and classical signatures. For visualization, we defined bins of low - lowest 25th percentile, medium - middle 50th percentile, and high - top 25th percentile signature expression.

#### Biomarkers for KRAS dependency

Cell lines were stratified into KRAS-dependent and -independent groups by CRISPR KO KRAS dependency score (top vs. bottom quartile). Differentially enriched genes were computed using a two-sided Mann-Whitney U test and the top 50 differentially expressed genes in the top vs. bottom quartile were used as signatures for KRAS sensitivity and resistance. To analyze biologic pathways associated with KRAS sensitivity and resistance, gene signatures were inputted into MSigDB with an FDR-adjusted Q-value of less than 0.05. MRTX1133 and RMC-6236 drug viability assays were performed in pooled format using barcoded cancer cell lines as previously described. 15,106 Briefly, cell lines were subjected to 5-day viability assay using concentrations of MRTX1133 diluted on an 8-point, 2-fold ascending dose range. Barcodes were sequenced and relative viability was computed to generate an AUC metric.

#### Evaluating tumor vs. normal tissue expression

Cell surface genes considered for analysis were taken from lists derived from predictions from mass spectrometry data (Cell Surface Protein Atlas 103 ). Enrichment of gene expression in pancreatic tumors relative to normal tissue was defined in two ways. First, enrichment scores (PDAC enrichment vs. normal tissues) were computed as the log2-fold ratio of a gene’s median expression (TPM) in TCGA PDAC tumors relative to its expression (TPM) in the fourth-highest expressing normal tissue (based on median values) from Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx). In essence, this allows for gene expression in three normal tissues to be unaccounted for. As evident from clinically-approved ADCs, some level of on-target, off-tumor toxicity may be tolerable depending on context. The normal tissue types in this analysis included the aortic artery, coronary artery, tibial artery, bladder, amygdala, anterior cingulate cortex (BA24), caudate (basal ganglia), cerebellar hemisphere, cerebellum, cortex, frontal cortex (BA9), hippocampus, hypothalamus, nucleus accumbens (basal ganglia), putamen (basal ganglia), spinal cord (cervical c-1), substantia nigra, sigmoid colon, transverse colon, gastroesophageal junction, esophageal mucosa, esophageal muscularis, atrial appendage of the heart, left ventricle of the heart, renal cortex, renal medulla, liver, lung, skeletal muscle, tibial nerve, pituitary, non-sun-exposed skin, sun-exposed skin, terminal ileum of the small intestines, stomach, and whole blood. Second, enrichment scores (PDAC enrichment vs. pancreas) were also computed as the log2-fold ratio of a gene’s median expression (TPM) in the TCGA PDAC cohort relative to its median expression (TPM) in normal pancreata from GTEx. Protein enrichment versus normal pancreatic tissue was calculated as a Z normalized log fold change using proteomics from the Clinical Proteomic Tumor Analysis Consortium. 85

#### Differential expression and heterogeneity analysis using snRNA-seq data

Cell-type annotations from a previously described snRNA-seq study of primary PDAC patient tumors were used. 72 In brief, community detection with the Leiden graph clustering method was performed on 40 principal components derived from the top 2,000 variably expressed genes in the dataset. Distinct cell populations, such as ductal cells, were then annotated with cell type-specific gene signatures and gene markers. Malignant cells were identified from a Python implementation of InferCNV v3.9, using non-malignant pancreas snRNA-seq samples as a non-cancerous reference. Annotated epithelial cells were sub-clustered with the Leiden method, and cells with an average CNA greater than 0.01 were annotated as malignant. Differential expression of prioritized CSP genes was computed as a percentile normalized statistic where the highest mean expression across cell types was assigned 1, and lowest expression was assigned 0. Expression values are count normalized on a per cell basis and log transformed prior to analysis. For assessment of co-expression of targets within the same cell and across populations, we counted the proportion of cells expressing each marker gene.

#### Single cell expression of target genes in critical normal healthy tissue

Single cell sequencing data from the Human Cell Atlas was retrieved from the CellxGene web browser (https://cellxgene.cziscience.com/gene-expression) for a set of toxicity prone healthy tissues (adrenal gland, bladder, blood, bone marrow, brain, breast, colon, endocrine gland, esophagus, exocrine gland, eye, heart, kidney, large intestine, liver, lung, lymph node, skeletal muscle, pancreas, prostate gland, skin, small intestine, spinal cord, spleen, stomach). We scored expression of a target gene in each organ by creating a metric based upon the proportion of a given cell type within the overall organ, the proportion of cells within the cell type expressing the target, and the relative expression of the target gene within that cell type. The product of these three factors was taken for each cell type within the tissue and the maximum score across all cell types, normalized by ACTB, was used for visualization. The goal of this approach was to maximize sensitivity for picking up high expression in rare cell types, while weighting expression overall in the tissue.

#### Cell surface targets associated with transcriptional state

To determine associations between cell surface target gene expression and classical and basal-like states,55 we computed the Pearson correlation coefficient between target expression and overall signature score as determined from single sample gene set enrichment analyses (ssGSEA). 105 These relationships were computed using gene expression data of PDAC cell lines, patient derived PDAC organoids from liver biopsies, and TCGA patients.

#### Whole transcriptome digital spatial profiling experiments and analysis

Whole transcriptome digital spatial profiling (DSP) of 18,269 mRNA targets was performed with the Nanostring GeoMx platform data of 21 PDAC patient specimens (IRB-approved protocol (2003P001289)) and are described in greater detail in a prior study. 72 In brief, tissue slides of FFPE sections were prepared, hybridized to an RNA in situ hybridization probe set comprised of 18,269 targets, and counterstained with morphology markers to designate distinct cell types. Cell-type protein markers included panCK for epithelial cells, CD45 for immune cells, and αSMA for fibroblasts. SYTO13 was used as a nuclear stain. The GeoMx Digital Spatial Profiling instrument from Nanostring was used to then select circular regions of interest (ROIs), segment into marker-defined areas of interest (AOIs) within, and collect barcodes for downstream sequencing. FASTQ files were distilled into count matrices as described previously. 72 Data were processed using upper quartile (Q3) normalization, and targets which consistently fell below a limit of quantitation were removed.

To evaluate distribution of target expression across ROIs and patients, inter- and intra-patient dispersion of gene expression was computed. To assess a gene’s expression within a patient, intra-patient dispersion was calculated as the patient-level mean of the interquartile range across each patient’s ROIs; conversely, to assess a gene’s expression across patients, inter-patient dispersion was calculated as the interquartile range of the mean expression for each patient. Interquartile range refers to the difference between the upper and lower quartile value. For visualization of target distribution across ROIs and patients, we binarized expression values to score each ROI as positive or negative by setting a cutoff based on each gene’s distribution. Malignant cell expression of a gene was considered positive if the expression was greater than the 80 th percentile of expression in adjacent non-malignant segments. The proportion of positive ROIs across the total number of ROIs sampled was computed and plotted for each patient and cell surface gene.

#### Co-dependency analysis

To identify genetic dependencies that may be co-targeted, we calculated a ‘combination dependency score’ by summing gene-wise pairs of Chronos dependency scores for each PDAC cell line and then taking the median across the PDAC cell lines for each gene pair. Using this combination dependency score, we recalculated the proportion of PDAC cell lines dependent on the combination (i.e., combination dependency score < − 0.5). The combination dependency score and proportion dependent for each of the resulting combination pairs was plotted. For visualization of dependencies in combination with KRAS, we filtered the pairs to only include genes in combination with KRAS and plotted the combination dependency score against the LRT selectivity score of the gene paired with KRAS. To identify cell surface targets that may combine well with genetic dependencies, we calculated Spearman correlation coefficients between TPM values and Chronos dependency score values across all PDAC cell lines profiled in the CCLE (n = 45). For pairs of genetic dependencies in the overlapping set between clinically tractable and PDAC selective targets, and prioritized CSP-encoding genes, we visualized correlation coefficients in a heatmap.

#### Transcriptional subtype-related cell surface target-specific cytoablation

PDAC organoids were cultured as previously described. 74 Briefly, cells were seeded into growth factor-reduced Matrigel (Corning; Cat. #356231) domes and incubated at 37 ◦ C in a 5% CO2 humidified incubator with human complete feeding medium.

For the viability assay, organoids were dissociated using TrypLE Express (Thermo Fisher Scientific; Cat. #12604054), and cells were seeded into ultra-low attachment 384-well plates (Corning; Cat. #4588) at 1,000 viable cells per well in 50 μL of culture media, consisting of 10% growth factor-reduced Matrigel and 90% human complete feeding medium. Humanized anti-TROP2 antibody datopotamab (MedChemExpress; Cat. #HY-P99843), human chimeric anti-CLDN18.2 antibody zolbetuximab (MedChemExpress; Cat. #HY-P99058), or human IgG1 isotype control antibody (Selleck; Cat. #A2051) was added at 9 to 11 concentrations, ranging from 0.01 to 100 nmol/L, in a randomized manner using a Tecan D300e Digital Dispenser (Tecan). Fab-αHFc-NC-MMAF, a Fab fragment of an anti-human IgG Fc-specific antibody conjugated to monomethyl auristatin F (Moradec; Cat. #AH-201-AF), was also added at a 1:3 molar ratio. Cell viability was assessed 3 days post-treatment using the Cell-TiterGlo 3D Cell Viability assay (Promega; Cat. #G9683), performed according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Luminescence signals were detected with a FLUOstar Omega microplate reader (BMG LABTECH) and normalized to non-treated wells. Three to five technical replicates were carried out for three independent biological replicates.

For cell surface staining, PDAC organoids were dissociated using TrypLE Express and stained with datopotamab, zolbetuximab, or the isotype control IgG1 in Flow Cytometry Staining Buffer (Thermo Fisher Scientific; Cat. #00–4222-26) for 1 h on ice. The cells were then stained with APC-labeled rat anti-human IgG Fc Antibody (BioLegend; Cat. #410712) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Data were acquired using an LSR Fortessa (BD) and analyzed with FlowJo (BD; version 10.9.0).

#### 2D cell lines and reagents

Human PDAC cell lines were obtained from the Broad Institute Cancer Dependency Map or American Type Culture Collection (ATCC). Authentication of cells was performed using STR DNA fingerprinting (Lab Corps). Cell lines were tested every 3 to 4 months and confirmed to be negative for mycoplasma using Mycostrip Mycoplasma Detection Kit (InvivoGene; Cat. # rep-mys-100) or via PCR (Labcorp). Cells were grown in the following media supplemented with 1% penicillin (Gibco) and 10% fetal bovine serum (Life Technologies): DMEM (PA-TU-8988T), RPMI 1640 (PANC 04.03, YAPC, KP-4, HuP_T4, BxPC-3, SNU-410, TCC-Pan2).

#### Generation of isogenic cell lines

Cell lines were infected with virus expressing CDS2 sgRNA, CDS1 sgRNA, or an intergenic control. Guide sequences were indicated in the table below. For infections of cells, 500,000 cells per well were seeded in 48-well plates with 250 μl media with 4 μg/ml of polybrene. 25–200μl of virus was added per well and spun for 2hr at 2250 rpm at 30 ◦ C. 6hrs post-infection, cells were split into a 6 cm dish. 24 h later, cells were selected with puromycin for one week.

#### CRISPR-based cell viability assays

#### Assay design and cell line optimization

CellTiter-Glo viability assays were performed with stably expressing lentiv2 cell lines in 96 well plates as previously described. 25 Cell lines were seeded and spinfected with sgRNA expressing lentivirus in wells on day 0 for 900 × g for 90 min 24 h post-infection, cells were selected with puromycin for 6 days. Cell titer-glo viability was readout 7 days after infection. Prior to infections, all cell lines were optimized for assay conditions including seeding densities and volumes of virus for each infection. All lentiviral preps for each sgRNA described were batch controlled and titrated on three different cell lines representing cell lines with low, medium, and high lentiviral transduction efficiency. Optimal cell seeding densities and viral volumes were used for all subsequent CRISPR-based viability assays.

#### sgRNAs design and rationale

For viability assays, we used 3 negative control guides (sgLacZ, sgAAVS1, and sgChr2), 3 positive control guides targeting pan-essential genes (sgKIF11, sgPOLR2D, and sgSF3B1), and 3 guides targeting CDS2 (sgCDS2–1, sgCDS2–2, and sgCDS2–3) as previously described. 25 For negative control guides, we design two “cutting controls” guides which allow CRISPR-SpCas9 cleaving safe regions of human genomes to control for DNA double-strand breaks. For sgChr2, the sgRNA targets a gene desert on chromosome 2, which is also the least copy number altered chromosome across cancer. 107 For sgAAVS1, this sgRNA targets the safe harbor of AAVS1 integration locus which is an intronic region in PPP1R12C. sgLacZ is a non-targeting sequence not found in the human genome. All sgRNA were cloned into a 3rd generation lentiviral vector (pXPR_023, Broad Institute) encoding for a human U6 promoter followed by hSpCas9 with chRNA backbone and puro-resistance marker. Lentiviral particles were generated by Lipofectamine 3000 (Thermo Fischer Scientific) transfection of sgRNA plasmids with ViralPower lentiviral packaging mix (Thermo Fischer Scientific) into HEK293T cells according to manufacturer’s protocol. sgRNA target sequences with cloning adapters were obtained from Integrated DNA technologies (IDT) as single stranded standard-desalted dsDNA oligos.

#### Viability assay data quality control

Each viability assay was performed to meet specific quality control parameters. There were 10 unique conditions, one for each of the 9 guides previously described above, plus a no infection control. Each sgRNA infection had 6 replicates, 3 of which were selected with puromycin and 4 that were not. For quality control of raw luminescence from CellTiter-Glo, we necessitated infection efficiency (puro/no puro selection for each guide) to be ∼80%, and all replicates had to be within 2 standard deviations of the mean for that sgRNA infection. We also accounted for viability reduction from cutting controls for DNA double-strand breaks to be no more than 30% of the non-targeting sgLacZ.

#### Viability assay data normalization

As previously described, 25 we wanted to normalize and scale the viability data in a manner comparable to the DepMap dependency scores. 45 Viability scores were normalized on a scale from 0 (average effect of negative sgRNA cutting controls) to − 1 (the average effect of knockout from 3 different pan-essential genes). We first calculated the distance of each well to the average to the two-cutting control sgRNAs (sgAAVS1 and sgChr2). We next scaled the values of each well from 0 to − 1 where 0 represents average viability effect of cutting controls and − 1 represents viability effect knockout of the 4 pan-essential genes. Scaling the cell viability in this manner permits one to compare across cell lines that have differential response to “off-target” effects from CRISPR and differential Cas9 activity when cell lines exhibit differences in maximum number of cells killed by pan-essential gene ablation.

#### Immunoblotting

Whole cell protein lysates were collected in cold RIPA buffer ( Thermo Fischer Scientific) supplemented with HALT protease and phosphatase cocktail (Thermo Fischer Scientific). Cell extracts were agitated for 30 min at 4◦ C and then spun for 16,000 × g for 20 min at 4◦ C. The protein concentration for each sample was then quantified via BCA Protein Assay Kit (Pierce) and diluted to desired concentrations. Lysates were then run on Bio-Rad Any kD mini-protean TGX protein gels and transferred to PVDF membranes (Bio-Rad). Membranes were incubated in primary antibodies overnight at 4◦ C, followed by HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies at room temperature for 1 h. The images were analyzed using ECL substrates (Pierce) under the ChemiDoc Imaging System (Bio-Rad).

#### siRNA transfections

Cells were seeded in a 96- or 6-well format. At Day 0, cells were reverse transfected with 10 nM siRNA and Lipofectamine RNAiMAX, according to manufacturer’s protocol. For RNAiduplex-Lipofectamine RNAiMAX complexes, diluted siRNAs in OptiMEM and RNAiMAX were prepared independently, combined, and then incubated for 15 min at room temperature. After incubations, complexes were added to cells. For 96-wells, cells were kept in knockdown until day 6. siRNA transfections were refreshed at day 3. At day 6, CellTiter glo viability assay was performed. For 6-wells, cells remained in knockdown and knockdown was confirmed by western blot 72-h post-transfection.

Three technical replicates were carried out for quantification of each experiment, indicated in the respective figure legend. Error bar reflects standard error of mean of all the technical replicates. The p-value was calculated using student T test.
